text: Why would a company hand some of its savings back to customers?
say: Why would a company hand some of its savings back to customers?

text: Hold that question. Rivals rush to copy a good business. A few are hard to copy: they have a moat, like water round a castle. Today: a castle with five gates. Experts count the kinds differently. This is our simple cut.
say: Hold that question. Rivals rush to copy a good business. A few are hard to copy: they have a moat, like water round a castle. Today: a castle with five gates. Experts count the kinds differently. This is our simple cut.

text: At each gate stands one Indian company. Every gate also hangs on a hinge, the one weak spot that could swing it open. For two of the five gates, a regulator, the official rule-setter, holds the hinge. Which two? Stay to the end.
say: At each gate stands one Indian company. Every gate also hangs on a hinge, the one weak spot that could swing it open. For two of the five gates, a regulator, the official rule-setter, holds the hinge. Which two? Stay to the end.

text: Gate one is a name people trust, and it answers our first question. Marico's oldest and largest product is Parachute Rigids. Copra, the raw material for coconut oil, got cheaper. Marico could have kept the saving as extra profit. It passed some on to shoppers. Did its sales suffer?

text: In its investor presentation of 4 August 2026, Marico said it took "selective price actions to pass on value to consumers." Selective. Not a cut on everything.
say: In its investor presentation of the fourth of August, twenty twenty-six, Marico said it took "selective price actions to pass on value to consumers." Selective. Not a cut on everything.

text: And the result? The same report says Parachute Rigids grew its volume 10%. Volume means how much was sold. Revenue grew 23%. Revenue means the money that came in. Revenue grew faster than volume, so prices did not fall across the board: the company says its price growth slowed. So why did shoppers keep buying?

text: Our article's reading: the brand can hold its customers on its own strength. Made-up example: you pick the same biscuit packet every week without checking the others. That habit is the gate. It is a brand moat. So why hand savings back?

text: Our article's answer: a trusted name can give price back when costs fall. It can raise price when costs rise. Shoppers read both as fair. The giveback is what makes the next price rise easier to accept.
say: Our article's answer: a trusted name can give price back when costs fall. It can raise price when costs rise. Shoppers read both as fair. The giveback is what makes the next price rise easier to accept.

text: But a name is only one gate. Gate two is about a thin profit. In the September quarter of 2026, DMart kept about ₹4 of profit after tax from every ₹100 it sold, by our arithmetic. Our article says that thin margin is by design: DMart sells mostly food and daily goods at low prices.
say: But a name is only one gate. Gate two is about a thin profit. In the September quarter of twenty twenty-six, DMart kept about four rupees of profit after tax from every hundred rupees it sold, by our arithmetic. Our article says that thin margin is by design: DMart sells mostly food and daily goods at low prices.

text: Why is thin a strength? DMart's promise is the lowest everyday price. Our article says it can keep that promise only if its own costs are the lowest. Our reading: a rival with higher costs would have to sell below its own cost to match.

text: A low price keeps customers. Gate three keeps them another way: it makes leaving hard. And it starts with a price tag that looks like a typo: ₹1 lakh.
say: A low price keeps customers. Gate three keeps them another way: it makes leaving hard. And it starts with a price tag that looks like a typo: one lakh rupees.

text: TCS runs technology for big companies. On 1 October 2026 it told the stock exchange about a deal with Best Buy. Our TCS article says TCS is taking over Best Buy's India technology centre, about 450 people, for ₹1 lakh. So what is TCS really buying?

text: Not just the team. A multi-year agreement to run it comes with it. Our article calls this a pattern: TCS takes over a client's in-house technology team and signs a long contract around it. That feeds the moat, our article says, because the client's own people and systems then sit inside TCS. Our reading: the price is small. The prize is the contract.

text: That is a lock. Our article says replacing TCS is slow and risky for the large clients whose core systems it runs. So why is leaving so hard? Made-up example: think of changing your salary account. The rent, the EMI and the light bill all pull money from that one account. Moving the account is easy. Moving everything hanging off it is the pain.

text: Gate four is the strangest, because here the crowd is the gate. The Indian Energy Exchange, IEX, runs auctions where electricity is bought and sold. Two rivals hold the very same licence as IEX, and have not dislodged it.

text: At an analyst meet on 24 July 2026, IEX's management said it has always held an 80 to 85% market share. So why can't a rival win some of that?
say: At an analyst meet on the twenty-fourth of July, twenty twenty-six, IEX's management said it has always held an eighty to eighty-five percent market share. So why can't a rival win some of that?

text: Made-up example: two vegetable markets side by side. One is packed. Sellers go where the buyers are, and buyers go where the sellers are. The empty one cannot start. A missed electricity trade cannot be saved and sold tomorrow, our article says, so everyone wants the market most likely to clear their trade. A rival can copy the technology. It cannot copy the crowd overnight.

text: How long would a rival need? An analyst asked on IEX's earnings call for the year to March 2026 whether rivals could replicate it within a few quarters. SN Goel of IEX answered: "They had 17 years to replicate this."

text: A crowd is one way. A permit is another. Gate five is a licence, and it sounds like the strongest gate of all. But watch who sets its price. It belongs to CDSL. Our article says every demat account in the country sits with CDSL or NSDL. A demat account is the locker where your shares are kept.

text: Our article also says a new company needs a licence that isn't being handed out. Made-up example: a town where only two bus permits will ever be issued. A third bus company can bring all the money it likes. No permit, no bus. Our article calls CDSL's crowd effect textbook too, but here we follow the licence.

text: Now the strange part. Our article of 9 August 2026 says that in the quarter before it, SEBI, the market regulator, cut a fee. The fee for creating a customer's KYC record fell from ₹20 to ₹5. The fee for fetching one fell too. KYC is just an identity check.

The fee for creating a customer's KYC record fell from twenty rupees to five rupees. The fee for fetching one fell too. KYC is just an identity check.

text: Our article puts two numbers side by side. CDSL's KYC subsidiary grew its revenue 22% compared with a year earlier. Yet its profit before the tax bill fell 4%. Our article's reason: the one who sets the price is not the company. Our reading: a licence keeps rivals out. It does not keep the regulator out.

Our article's reason: the one who sets the price is not the company. Our reading: a licence keeps rivals out. It does not keep the regulator out.

text: Now the hinges. Two are held by a regulator. You have just seen gate five's: the fee table, which SEBI writes. The other is gate four's.

text: In April 2026, the electricity regulator published draft rules. They would pool the bids of every power exchange and clear them at one price, run by one operator, Grid-India. IEX would keep its customer relationships. But our article says the crowd itself would become common property. IEX's 2026 annual report says the impact would be minimal. Our article is not so sure. As of 5 October 2026, the rules were not final.

text: Now the other three. Gate one's hinge: the day coconut gets dearer again. Can Marico take price back and keep its shoppers? Falling costs are the easy case, and we have only one quarter of evidence.

text: Gate two's hinge: do the new stores fill up? In the year to March 2026, DMart added 85 stores, after four years of 40 to 50. Sales for each square foot of shop dipped that year. If the new stores do not fill up, DMart's low-cost edge gets thinner.
say: Gate two's hinge: do the new stores fill up? In the year to March twenty twenty-six, DMart added eighty-five stores, after four years of forty to fifty. Sales for each square foot of shop dipped that year. If the new stores do not fill up, DMart's low-cost edge gets thinner.

text: Gate three's hinge is a catch: the next contract. Our article says a lock protects the clients already inside, not the ones yet to sign. And our TCS article warns that AI may shrink the old work faster than the new work grows.

text: So, the verdict. Our test: a moat is proven when rivals try and fail, not when a company has a good year. In our articles from July to October 2026, all five gates are holding. Only gate four shows rivals trying and failing. Gate one rests on a single quarter, so it is the least proven. And a gate that holds is not the same as profit that stays. CDSL showed that.

text: Our reading: the first three hinges hang on customers. Will shoppers accept a price rise? Will new stores fill? Will the next contract be signed? The last two hang on a regulator. So when anyone says a company has a moat, ask two things. Where is the gate? And who holds the hinge?
